title: Prefer Header for HTTP
summary: Defines the Prefer HTTP header field, which a client uses to ask a server to behave in certain ways while handling a request. The server is free to ignore the preferences.

plainLanguage.summary: The Prefer header lets a client say "if you can, please do it this way" while handling a request. The server may ignore the wish, and a separate response header tells the client which wishes were actually followed.

questions: how to ask a server for a preferred behavior
what does prefer return minimal do
subtitle: Lets an HTTP client ask for optional server behaviour, knowing the server may ignore the request.

tldr.problem: HTTP had no way for a client to say how it would like a request handled: whether to wait or answer immediately, whether to get the whole resource back or just a confirmation, whether small errors should be forgiven.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a Prefer request header field carrying preference tokens with optional parameters, a Preference-Applied response header saying which preferences were honoured, and a registry of initial tokens.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from June 2014, updated by RFC 8144, and it is the standard way for a client to express an optional preference in HTTP.

today: RFC 7240 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2014. It is updated by RFC 8144 and has not been obsoleted, so the Prefer and Preference-Applied header fields remain the standard way to express an optional HTTP preference.

sections.title: Why a New Header for Preferences
sections.content:
Servers that process requests often face two kinds of decision. The first is what to return: after a successful modification, a server may return a representation of the modified resource or a minimal response indicating only successful completion. Which one to return generally has no bearing on successful processing of the request, but it can affect what the client must do afterwards, because returning the representation can save the client a further GET request. The second is how forgiving to be: a request may be technically invalid or incorrect but still understandable, and the server may be able to overlook the errors and process it successfully. Whether that leniency suits the application is something the client may care about.

While the decision of which behaviour to apply lies with the server, the server might wish to defer to the client to say which optional behaviour is preferred. HTTP offered no defined means of doing that. The Expect header could in principle be used, but it is a poor fit. Its semantics require intermediaries and servers to reject any request stating an unrecognised or unsupported expectation, and although it is end to end, the HTTP specification requires it to be processed hop by hop, so every intermediary has to decide whether it can handle the expectation. The must-understand semantics of Expect make it a poor choice for optional preferences. Request URI query-string parameters are another option, but any mechanism that alters the URI can have undesirable effects, such as when caches record the altered URI.

The document therefore defines a new HTTP request header field that a client can use to request that optional behaviours be applied during the processing of a request, plus a handful of initial preference tokens for use with it.
sections.plainLanguage: Existing HTTP headers were the wrong shape for this. Expect means "you must", and it has to be checked at every hop. A query string changes the address that caches remember. Prefer is a new field that is simply a wish.

sections.title: The Syntax of the Prefer Header
sections.content:
The Prefer request header field indicates that particular server behaviours are preferred by the client but are not required for successful completion of the request. It is similar in nature to the Expect header field, with the exception that servers are allowed to ignore stated preferences. Its syntax is Prefer = "Prefer" ":" 1#preference, where a preference is a token optionally followed by a word after an equals sign, and then any number of parameters, each of which is a token optionally followed by a word after an equals sign. The syntax is extensible so that future values can be added to the Registry of Preferences.

A server that does not recognise, or is unable to comply with, particular preference tokens in the Prefer header field of a request MUST ignore those tokens and continue processing instead of signalling an error. Empty or zero-length values on both the preference token and within parameters are equivalent to no value being specified at all, so Prefer: foo; bar, Prefer: foo; bar="" and Prefer: foo=""; bar are equivalent. An optional set of parameters can be specified for any preference token, and their meaning depends on the definition of that token and on the server's implementation. There is no significance in the ordering of parameters on any given preference. For both preference token names and parameter names, comparison is case insensitive, while values are case sensitive whether they are token or quoted-string values.
sections.plainLanguage: The header holds a list of named wishes, each with optional settings. A server that does not know a wish just ignores it; the request still goes through.

sections.title: Proxies, Repeats and Caching
sections.content:
The Prefer header field is end to end and MUST be forwarded by a proxy if the request is forwarded, unless Prefer is explicitly identified as hop by hop using the Connection header field. In various situations a proxy might determine that it can honour a preference independently of the server to which the request was directed. For instance, an intervening proxy might be capable of providing asynchronous handling of a request using 202 responses independently of the origin server, and such a proxy can choose to honour the respond-async preference on its own whether or not the origin is able or willing to do so. Individual preference tokens MAY define their own requirements and restrictions on whether and how intermediaries can apply the preference independently of the origin server.

A client MAY use multiple instances of the Prefer header field in a single message, or a single field with multiple comma-separated preference tokens. Multiple fields are equivalent to one field holding the comma-separated concatenation of all the tokens. To avoid ambiguity, individual preference tokens SHOULD NOT appear more than once in a single request; if a preference is specified more than once, only the first instance is considered and the later ones SHOULD be ignored without signalling an error or otherwise altering the processing of the request. This is the only case in which the ordering of preferences within a request is significant.

Because of the complexities involved in server-driven content negotiation, effective caching and the application of optional preferences, implementers are urged to exercise caution when using preferences in a way that affects caching, and SHOULD NOT use the Prefer mechanism for content negotiation. If a server supports the optional application of a preference that might result in a variance in a cache's handling of a response entity, a Vary header field MUST be included in the response listing the Prefer header field, regardless of whether the client actually used Prefer in the request. Alternatively the server MAY include a Vary header with the special value "*", but that will make it impossible for a proxy to cache the response. Preference tokens are similar in structure to HTTP Expect tokens, but the two header fields serve very distinct purposes and preferences cannot be used as expectations.
sections.plainLanguage: The header travels the whole way to the server. If the answer depends on the wish, the server must say so in a Vary header so that caches do not mix up the answers.

sections.title: The Preference-Applied Response Header
sections.content:
The Preference-Applied response header MAY be included in a response message to indicate which Prefer tokens were honoured by the server and applied to the processing of the request. Its syntax is Preference-Applied = "Preference-Applied" ":" 1#applied-pref, where an applied preference is a token optionally followed by a word after an equals sign. The syntax differs from that of the Prefer header in that parameters are not included.

Using the header is only necessary when it is not readily and obviously apparent that the server applied a given preference, and such ambiguity might affect how the client handles the response. For instance, with the return=representation or return=minimal preferences, a client application might not be able to tell reliably from the response payload alone whether the preference was applied. In the example given, a PATCH request carries Prefer: return=representation and the response carries Preference-Applied: return=representation together with a Content-Location header and the representation itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the answer does not reveal whether the server did what was asked. This response header says so explicitly, without repeating the settings.

sections.title: The Preference Tokens
sections.content:
respond-async indicates that the client prefers the server to respond asynchronously. For instance, where the time needed to generate a response will exceed some threshold the server has set, the server can honour the preference by returning a 202 response. The motivation is to let a client indicate its capability and preference for handling asynchronous responses. While the 202 status is defined in RFC 7231, little guidance is given on how and when to use it, and the process for determining the subsequent final result is left undefined, so whether and how any given server supports asynchronous responses is an implementation-specific detail outside the scope of the specification.

return=representation indicates that the client prefers the server to include an entity representing the current state of the resource in the response to a successful request. The returned representation might not be one of the effective request URI when the request affects another resource, in which case the Content-Location header can identify the URI of the returned representation. The point is to optimise communication by removing the need for a subsequent GET request after a modification. return=minimal indicates that the client wants only a minimal response, typically using the 204 status, though other codes MAY be used such as a 200 with a zero-length response entity; what counts as an appropriate minimal response is solely at the discretion of the server. The two return preferences are mutually exclusive, and a request containing both can be treated as though neither were specified.

wait establishes an upper bound, in seconds, on the time the client expects the server to take to process the request once received. Where generating a response will take longer, the server or proxy can choose to use an asynchronous processing model, for example by returning a 202 response. HTTP messages spend some time traversing the network and being processed by intermediaries, which adds to the time the client waits, so a client with strict timing requirements can estimate those factors and adjust the value. As with other preferences, wait could be ignored, and clients can abandon requests that take longer than they are prepared to wait.

handling=strict and handling=lenient indicate, at the server's discretion, how the client wishes the server to handle potential error conditions. If the payload of a request contains minor syntactic or semantic errors but the server can still comprehend and process it, a decision must be made to reject the request with an appropriate 4xx response or go ahead. handling=strict says the client would prefer rejection; handling=lenient says the client wants the server to attempt to process the request. They are mutually exclusive, and a request containing both can be treated as though neither were specified.
sections.plainLanguage: Four wishes are defined: answer now or later, give me the whole thing or just an acknowledgement, how long I can wait, and whether small mistakes should be forgiven.

sections.title: The Registry of Preferences
sections.content:
The Prefer and Preference-Applied header fields have been added to the Permanent Message Header Field Names registry, both with the status Standard and the IETF as change controller.

IANA has created a new registry, HTTP Preferences, under the Hypertext Transfer Protocol Parameters registry. New registrations use the Specification Required policy of RFC 5226, and the requirements for registered preferences are those of Section 4. A registration request consists of the preference value, its possible values, its optional parameters, a description, a reference and optional notes. The Value and Optional Parameters fields MAY be omitted when the definition of the preference does not have them.

To allow values to be allocated before publication, the Designated Expert can approve a registration based on a separately submitted template once satisfied that a specification will be published. Preferences can also be registered by third parties if the Designated Expert determines that an unregistered preference is widely deployed and not likely to be registered in a timely manner. Within at most 14 days of a request the Designated Expert will approve or deny it, communicating the decision to the review list and IANA, and denials should include an explanation and, where applicable, suggestions for making the request successful.

The Expert Reviewer must ensure that the requested name conforms to the token rule and is not identical to another registered name, that any values and parameter names conform to the grammar, that the name is appropriate to the specificity of the preference so that more general names stay available for less specific uses, that the preference does not constrain servers, clients or intermediaries to any behaviour required for successful processing, and that the defining specification includes a proper and complete discussion of the security considerations. The initial registry contents are respond-async, return with the values minimal and representation, wait, and handling with the values strict and lenient.
sections.plainLanguage: New wishes can be registered with IANA, and the reviewers check that each one is well named, does not demand anything essential, and has its security notes written down.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Specific preferences requested by a client can introduce security considerations beyond those discussed in HTTP/1.1 (RFC 7230) and its associated documents. Implementers need to refer to the specifications and descriptions of each preference to determine the security considerations relevant to it.

A server could incur greater costs in attempting to comply with a particular preference, for instance the cost of providing a representation in a response that would not ordinarily contain one, or the commitment of resources necessary to track state for an asynchronous response. Unconditional compliance from a server could allow preferences to be used for denial of service. A server can ignore an expressed preference to avoid expending resources it does not wish to commit.
sections.plainLanguage: Doing what the client asks can cost the server money, so the server is always allowed to say no, and that is one of the main safety valves here.

data.title: Request with a Prefer header
data.code:
POST /collection HTTP/1.1
Host: example.org
Content-Type: text/plain
Prefer: respond-async, wait=10
Prefer: priority=5
